title: Matrix Norms, Conditioning and Perturbation

intro.x: Real computations use approximate numbers: measurements are noisy and floating-point arithmetic rounds. How much can the answer to a linear algebra problem change when the data change slightly? Whether a problem is well-conditioned (small data errors cause small answer errors) is a property of the problem, independent of the algorithm; whether an algorithm is stable is a property of the method. This chapter develops the tools, matrix norms and the condition number, and applies them to linear systems, eigenvalues and least squares. These ideas decide whether a numerical result can be trusted.

blocks.x: Chapter 1 defined vector norms. For matrices we want a size function $\norm{A}$ that behaves well under products.

The spectral radius $\rho(A)=\max\abs{\lambda_i}$ satisfies $\rho(A)\le\norm{A}$ for every induced norm. Moreover $\norm{A^k}^{1/k}\to\rho(A)$ as $k\to\infty$ (Gelfand’s formula), so $A^k\to0$ iff $\rho(A)<1$.

The Neumann series and perturbation of the inverse
If $\norm{E}<1$ in some induced norm, then $I-E$ is invertible,
(I-E)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty E^k,\qquad\norm{(I-E)^{-1}}\le\frac1{1-\norm{E}}.

The $n\times n$ Hilbert matrix $H_{ij}=1/(i+j-1)$ is symmetric positive definite and spectacularly ill-conditioned: $\kappa_2(H_5)\approx4.8\times10^5$, $\kappa_2(H_{10})\approx1.6\times10^{13}$, and $\kappa_2(H_n)$ grows like $e^{3.5n}$. In double precision ($\varepsilon\approx10^{-16}$) one cannot solve $H_{12}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ with any accuracy, no matter how clever the algorithm: the problem is ill-conditioned.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: conditioning belongs to the problem, stability to the algorithm

blocks.x: A backward stable algorithm returns the exact answer for a slightly perturbed input $A+E$ with $\norm{E}/\norm{A}=O(\varepsilon)$. Combining this with Theorem 18.9, the forward relative error is $O(\kappa(A)\varepsilon)$. So a good algorithm cannot beat the conditioning of the problem, and a stable algorithm gives nearly optimal accuracy. $LU$ with partial pivoting, QR with Householder reflections and the SVD are backward stable; the normal equations are not backward stable for least squares because $\kappa(A\T A)=\kappa(A)^2$.

For full-column-rank $A$, the squared condition number appears in sensitivity: the relative error in $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is bounded roughly by $\kappa(A)\epsilon_{rel}+\kappa(A)^2\tan\theta\,\epsilon_{rel}$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\mathbf{b}$ and $\Col A$. For consistent systems ($\theta=0$) the conditioning is $\kappa(A)$; for large residuals it is $\kappa(A)^2$.
Let $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ be diagonalisable. For every eigenvalue $\mu$ of $A+E$ there is an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ with
\abs{\mu-\lambda}\le\kappa(V)\,\norm{E}.

For normal matrices $V$ can be chosen unitary with $\kappa(V)=1$, so perturbing a normal (in particular a symmetric) matrix by $\varepsilon$ moves eigenvalues by at most $\varepsilon$ (Weyl, Theorem 15.9). For non-normal matrices $\kappa(V)$ can be huge, so eigenvalues can be very sensitive; defective matrices ($V$ singular) are the extreme case.

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1000\\0&1+10^{-6}\end{pmatrix}$, nearly defective. Eigenvalues $1$ and $1+10^{-6}$; the matrix of eigenvectors is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&10^{-9}\end{pmatrix}$ with condition number about $10^9$. Changing the $(2,1)$ entry from $0$ to $\delta=10^{-10}$ replaces the eigenvalue equation by $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-1-10^{-6})=1000\delta$, whose roots now differ by about $6\times10^{-4}$: the eigenvalues move by roughly $3\times10^{-4}$, millions of times more than the perturbation.

Because (i) their eigenvalues are real, (ii) there is an orthogonal eigenbasis with $\kappa=1$, so by Bauer–Fike / Weyl eigenvalue errors are bounded by the data error, and (iii) algorithms such as Jacobi, QR iteration and divide-and-conquer are backward stable and accurate. Non-symmetric eigenproblems are genuinely harder, and defective cases are ill-posed.

Double precision stores a number with about $16$ decimal digits; the unit roundoff is $u\approx1.1\times10^{-16}$. Each elementary operation returns $\mathrm{fl}(a\circ b)=(a\circ b)(1+\delta)$ with $\abs{\delta}\le u$. Rounding errors have three practical consequences for linear algebra.
Subtracting nearly equal numbers destroys relative accuracy (cancellation). Computing $b^2-4ac$ when $b^2\approx4ac$, or $\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{y}$ for nearly orthogonal vectors, loses digits.
Dividing by small pivots amplifies earlier errors, motivating pivoting (Chapter 4).
Algebraically equivalent formulas are not numerically equivalent. Solving $(A\T A)\mathbf{x}=A\T\mathbf{b}$ and using QR agree in exact arithmetic but differ by a factor $\kappa(A)$ in accuracy.

Take $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\\varepsilon&0\\0&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}$ with $\varepsilon=10^{-9}$. In exact arithmetic $A$ has independent columns, but $A\T A=\begin{pmatrix}1+\varepsilon^2&1\\1&1+\varepsilon^2\end{pmatrix}$ rounds to $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ in double precision (because $\varepsilon^2=10^{-18}<u$), which is singular. QR sees the two columns as distinct and succeeds.
